Sample.warning: The sample size (total_n) was not reported in this section.

Area.evidence_source: All participants described experiencing predominantly negative feelings and having difficulty with emotional expression. Intense negative emotions were kept private or expressed inappropriately. As teens, they often lacked a developed vocabulary to talk about feelings. They spoke of feeling pain constantly, not being able to differentiate between emotional states, or not knowing what they were feeling. Many simply said they felt "sad" or "depressed" and had difficulty articulating distinct emotions. Participants used metaphors such as "a dark place," "a yucky cloud," "an abyss," or "the crud under somebody's shoe" to describe their emotional experiences and feelings. Extreme discomfort with having such intense, yet indescribable, feelings was identified. Anger was commonly identified as the prevailing emotion used by participants to communicate their internal experience. For many, anger was the only emotion expressed and it became a safe way to show the world some of the negativity that dominated their lives. Anger was directed inward, at those around them, and at the world in general. These teens identified defiance, rebellion, explosiveness, irritability, hostility, and violence as mechanisms designed to mask their internal suffering. Most often, anger was the tool of expression used to hide underlying despair, fear, insecurity, and helplessness. Many participants described a confusion created by the chaos of their emotional state; they did not know how to feel or what to do with the emotions they were containing. Ruminating on their feelings of despair and becoming overpowered by pain and problems was commonly reported. Emotional pain was perceived as taking over every aspect of their lives and participants believed that they had no control over how they were feeling. Participants' lack of familiarity with positive emotions created a perception that happiness was impossible. Furthermore, confusion arose when positive emotions were experienced because this was incongruent with their developed perception of self. Many, therefore, found themselves with a selfimposed restriction on positive emotional states. Being suicidal was kind of my safety zone. If I had a good day and I found myself being positive I wasn't really sure what to do. So it was almost like I had to find something to make myself feel bad, because that's how I was used to feeling. Participants became completely focused on suicide as the only means of ridding themselves of emotional pain. Thinking about suicide became a means of coping. Often, these adolescents spent hours visualizing and planning their suicide and the consequences of their death and reported momentary relief in their suicidal fantasies. Adaptive strategies for coping with difficult emotions appeared to be lacking. Several participants who tried to manage their affect reported using a limited repertoire of maladaptive strategies that, for the most part, included cutting, self-harming behaviors, and eating disorders. When feelings got too intense, other means of escape and avoidance to get a break from the pain included partying, abusing drugs and alcohol, being sexually promiscuous, and creating a chaotic lifestyle. These strategies were reported to be temporarily useful but ineffective in resolving difficult emotions. Few teens talked about having any positive coping strategies, and those who did used them infrequently. I was hurting and I don't know whether it released the anger or released the pain. I was in a lot of pain. I remember just cutting and cutting and cutting and dipping my wrists in hot water and just lying there. . . . I was cutting myself continually. It was constant. Many participants attributed difficulties with emotional expression and poorly developed emotional control to parent–child interactions. Participants reported family environments in which parents did not show emotions or discuss feelings and personal issues. In addition, participants perceived their relationships with parents to lack the closeness, intimacy, and trust necessary for open and honest personal disclosures. Without healthy modeling at home, these participants felt limited in their capacity to adaptively regulate emotions. I don't think I was trained to share my emotions. In my family definitely, we were discouraged to show emotions and I think that's probably a lot of the problem. Despite a strong desire to let their parents know how they were feeling, participants described being fearful of parental reaction to the expression of negative emotions because of the concern about being ridiculed, criticized, belittled, or punished when intimate feelings and personal problems were shared. Parents were also perceived as having a low tolerance for negative emotion. When participants displayed negative affect, they felt that their feelings were denied or distorted. They reported the perception that real feelings were dismissed or minimized and believed that the only acceptable feeling they could express in the home was happiness. As they believed that communication of emotions was not valued, participants learned that there was no point in talking about feelings. As participants struggled with powerful suicidal feelings, limited emotional communication with parents affected their ability to directly reach out for help. I wasn't used to sharing my feelings because I'd never really had feelings, because I wasn't really allowed. I was told how to feel my entire life. Participants often interpreted their lack of emotional communication and expression with their parents as an indicator that they were unimportant family members or that their parents did not care. The perception of the unavailability of parental emotional support left many participants feeling unloved and rejected. However, most expressed a desire for closer connection and understanding with parents, although this appeared, at the time, to be an unattainable goal. Relationships with parents were described as having a strong influence on participants' abilities to successfully deal with emotional difficulties. Most participants assumed an artificial emotional identity while suicidal by keeping true feelings hidden from those around them. As they did not feel safe enough to reveal their despair to family or friends, many pretended to be happy and created a false mask for protection. Participants struggled with, and felt conflicted by, having two distinct personas: a public and a private self. In public, participants felt that they needed to show strength and described feeling uncomfortable crying or displaying difficult emotions. While suicidal, these individuals reported feeling invisible because no one knew how they were truly feeling. I was just going through the motions, showing everyone a happy side of me when I felt awful on the inside. As they became increasingly suicidal, many participants expressed a decline in initiative to socialize and be with other people. Most participants did not know how to establish a relationship with others who would be emotionally available to them and help them handle their feelings. They were insecure in their ability to cope and to create supportive connections.
